<meta>continues from previous page</meta>the animal. <margin>On the nature of the tiger caught.</margin> Under the compulsion of necessity, an art was finally invented by which it might pay the penalty for shedding so much blood. Having scouted the narrow paths and the hidden caves from which it was accustomed to go out at night for prey, a path was cut. They dug a pit, covered it with hurdles and the excavated earth—scattering the excess soil <margin>concerning the tiger</margin>—and leveled it. An incautious tiger, which was a male, came along and fell into the pit, where it became impaled on sharp stakes fixed at the bottom of the ditch. With its roaring, it deafened the entire neighborhood, and the mountains echoed with that shrieking. It was killed by casting huge stones and stakes fixed into the edges of the pit down upon it. It broke into a thousand splinters and a thousand fragments the spears held in right hands and those hurled from above. Even half-dead and bloodless, it filled those watching with fear, wondering what it might have done if it were free and unharmed. A certain Juan de Ledesma of Seville, a friend of Vasco <note>Vasco Núñez de Balboa</note> and a companion in his labors, confessed that he had eaten of that tiger. He reported to me that it was no worse than beef. When asked why they call it a tiger, those who have now seen the tiger respond that they judge it to be a tiger from its spots, its ferocity, its agility, and other signs given by authors; although many of them claim to have seen both leopards and panthers which are also spotted. After the male tiger was killed, they followed its tracks toward the mountains and reached the bridal cave that was its home.

From there they took two cubs, not yet old enough for their mother's teats. Changing their plan, they decided to return the little ones to the mother's cave with iron chains carefully fitted around their necks, so that they might later send them to Spain once they had grown larger. Returning to the cave a few days later, they found the cave empty, with the chains unmoved from their place. It is thought the mother, out of rage, tore them to pieces and carried them off so that no one might enjoy them. For they assert that there was no way they could have been released from the chains alive. The skin of the killed tiger was stuffed with dried herbs and straw and sent to Hispaniola for the Admiral <note>likely Diego Columbus</note> and the leading men, from whom these laws and aid for the new land are expected. Both those who suffered hardships from the tiger and those who handled its skin related these things to me; I receive what is given. We must return to Pacra, from whom we have diverged. Having entered the abandoned <term>boios</term> <gloss>huts or houses</gloss> of Pacra, Vasco endeavored to draw Pacra to him. Through messengers, <margin>Pacra returns</margin> he signaled the same things to Pacra that we have mentioned were signaled to the others. For a long time Pacra refused. Threats were added to his refusal. He finally came, accompanied by three petty kings. Vasco writes that Pacra was so deformed, filthy, and foul that he confesses he never saw anything more shameful. <margin>What Pacra is like; he is considered a Hercules.</margin> He says that nature gave him only a human form; otherwise, he was a wild, monstrous, brute animal. He says his character was equal to his appearance and features. By force, he had abducted the daughters of four neighboring petty kings and was abusing them with detestable lust. Many other things of this sort concerning the obscene habits and countless crimes of Pacra were boasted of by the neighboring petty kings in the presence of Vasco, as if before a praetorian judge or a Hercules-like avenger, so that punishment might be taken upon Pacra. He cast the massive beast <margin>concerning the punishment against the wicked.</margin> along with those three petty kings who were obedient to Pacra’s word and suffering from the same vices, into the jaws of war dogs, and he ordered their torn corpses to be burned. Miraculous things are related concerning the dogs with which they enter battles. <margin>wonders concerning the dogs.</margin> Against armed natives, they are quite fierce: there was no need for swords or arrows or other weapons to rout the opposing enemies; for once the signal was given and the dogs were released, the column, terrified by the appearance and unusual barking of the Molossian dogs, would hesitate and, in confusion, abandon their battle lines and orders. It happens differently, however, when they engage with the Caramairenses and Caribs; for they are fiercer and more apt at waging wars. Charging, they aim their poisoned arrows at the dogs faster than a lightning strike and kill many. The inhabitants of these mountains, however, do not wage war with arrows; <margin>with what arms they wage war</margin> they act against their enemies only with <term>maccanae</term> <gloss>wooden swords</gloss>, which are broad and oblong, and with missiles and fire-hardened spears. From the living Pacra, it could never be extorted by any enticements, threats, or tortures where his associates collected gold. When asked where he obtained it—for thirty pounds of gold <margin>30 pounds of gold from Pacra</margin> had been obtained from his treasury—he answered that his associates who used to collect gold from those mountains in the time of his parents and his own were dead. He claimed that he had not cared about seeking gold since he reached puberty. He could never be moved from this stated resolve. <summary>This page describes the capture and killing of a predatory tiger in the New World and the trial and execution of the local chieftain Pacra by Vasco Núñez de Balboa. It details the use of war dogs in Spanish conquests and the native refusal to disclose the sources of their gold.</summary>
